analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal for employers to agree not to hire or recruit each other's workers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate committee it was referred to, without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When companies agree not to poach each other's employees, workers lose the bargaining power that comes from being able to take a better offer elsewhere, which pushes wages down. This bill would make such agreements illegal, let the Federal Trade Commission enforce the ban, and let workers sue the companies for actual and punitive damages plus attorney's fees. It also covers no-poach terms buried in franchise and subcontractor contracts, which is how most fast-food and staffing firms impose them.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, especially the tens of millions in fast food, retail, staffing, and other low-wage, high-turnover industries where no-poach and wage-fixing agreements are common. They would gain the legal right to switch jobs freely and to sue employers who locked them in, recovering actual and punitive damages and attorney's fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers in franchise and staffing industries

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for any employer to enter into, enforce, or threaten to enforce an agreement that restricts another employer from hiring or soliciting its workers or former workers.

It reaches agreements imposed through franchise and contractor-subcontractor contracts, the main vehicle by which large brands keep franchisee employees from moving between locations or to competitors.
Workers would get a private right of action to recover actual damages, punitive damages as the court allows, and attorney's fees, giving them a direct way to fight back without waiting for an agency.
The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban with the full powers it has under the Federal Trade Commission Act, adding federal policing on top of private lawsuits.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on no-poach clauses to hold down turnover and wages, particularly franchise brands and staffing firms, which would lose a tool for suppressing labor costs and could face damages suits and FTC penalties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Franchise brands and employers using no-poach agreements

drawbacks.text: Businesses argue that some hiring restrictions are legitimate: franchise systems say brand-wide no-poach rules help fund training and prevent rival chains from free-riding on an investment in a trained workforce, and the bill would ban even those agreements with no carve-out.

The bill already overlaps with antitrust law, where courts and the Justice Department have pursued wage-fixing and no-poach deals as criminal violations, so some of the intended protection exists under existing law even without this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and large for ordinary workers: no-poach and wage-fixing agreements demonstrably hold down pay in exactly the industries where wages are lowest. The main cost falls on employers' ability to control labor costs, and the strongest objection, that legitimate franchise training arrangements get swept in, is real but narrow; Congress could have written a carve-out. On balance the public benefit substantially outweighs the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law, and nothing further ever happened to it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the End Employer Collusion Act in the Senate on March 1, 2018, with Senator Elizabeth Warren joining as an original co-sponsor.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

It had only one cosponsor beyond its original sponsors, and the committee took no further action, so the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use no-poach and wage-fixing agreements, particularly national franchise chains and staffing firms, are better off, because the practice stays legal and workers gained no new right to sue.

sides.party_line_note: All identified support came from Democrats, with just one cosponsor listed, and no Republican support appears in the record; the bill died in committee with the Senate under Republican control.

industries.industry: Franchise chains (fast food, retail, and services)
industries.note: Many large franchise brands impose no-poach terms in their franchise contracts, limiting where workers can move and holding down wages across the system. The bill would ban these terms and expose brands to damages suits and FTC enforcement.
The industry relies on agreements restricting firms from hiring each other's placed or assigned workers. The bill would make such agreements unlawful and let workers sue.
Any employer using no-poach or wage-fixing arrangements would face liability for actual and punitive damages plus attorney's fees, and would lose a tool for suppressing labor costs.
